conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in today because of a bad headache and high blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. My blood pressure was 220 over 110 at my doctor’s office. The headache has been going on for over a week—it’s like my usual migraines, but much worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned it's a throbbing pain in the front of your head and you're sensitive to light?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. No nausea or vomiting this time, but it’s constant and exhausting. I even had a brief episode of weakness on my right side a week ago, but the neurologist cleared me then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for that. We’ve reviewed your records. You have a history of migraines, high blood pressure from primary hyperaldosteronism, pseudotumor cerebri, and sleep apnea—all of which can play a role here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and my blood pressure has been hard to control. I’ve tried several meds, but they make me feel tired or too low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you’re on amlodipine and propranolol. We gave you labetalol in the ER to bring your pressure down. Your CT scan of the head was normal—no bleeding or stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But the headache is still really bad. The Dilaudid helped a little more than morphine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to keep monitoring your blood pressure and pain. We also did a chest X-ray and EKG—both were stable. No signs of heart strain or fluid in the lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did have chest tightness on the train this morning. It went to my left shoulder, but no sweating or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your cardiac enzymes three times—no sign of a heart attack. Given your normal stress test and angiogram in the past, it’s likely not cardiac. Probably related to anxiety or muscle tension.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been under a lot of stress lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding captopril to help control your blood pressure. It’s a different type of blood pressure med that might work better with your hyperaldosteronism.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken lisinopril before and it made me so tired. I had to stop it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Captopril is similar, but we’ll start low and monitor. If it causes fatigue, we’ll switch to enalapril, which you might tolerate better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds fair.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood pressure is coming down—now 158 over 90. But you’re still having headaches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, still pretty bad. I’m taking the Tylenol and oxycodone, but it’s not fully helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Neurology reviewed your case. Since your headache didn’t improve with blood pressure control and your eye exam is normal, it’s unlikely to be pseudotumor cerebri.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s still a migraine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. But we can’t use triptans because you’re on Celexa and have heart risk factors. NSAIDs are out because of your allergy. So we’re sticking with Tylenol and short-term oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I wish there was something more effective. The nasal Stadol my old neurologist used to prescribe helped a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We looked into that. Unfortunately, it’s very expensive and not covered under your plan. We’ll get you an appointment with your former neurologist to discuss long-term options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that would be good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, your EKG shows a prolonged QT interval. You’re on three medications that can affect this: Celexa, Topamax, and tizanidine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tizanidine is for muscle spasms in my neck. I take it at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think the benefits of Celexa and Topamax outweigh the risks, so we’re going to stop the tizanidine to protect your heart rhythm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I rely on it for sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor you. If the spasms come back, we can try other options. But your heart rhythm is a bigger concern right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is now 132 over 84—much better. And your headache is improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely better since last night. I’m still taking the oxycodone, but less often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to switch you from captopril to enalapril once a day. It’s the same class but easier to take and less likely to cause fatigue for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about the propranolol? I remember you said my heart rate was slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your heart rate was in the 50s. We held the propranolol for now. We’ll restart it once daily instead of twice, since it also helps prevent migraines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds okay. I don’t want to feel dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your blood pressure has been stable between 110 and 130 over 80. Your discharge is approved for today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What meds will I be going home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting enalapril once daily for blood pressure, stopping tizanidine, and reducing propranolol to once daily. You’ll take Tylenol as needed and a short course of oxycodone—just four days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—like Topamax and acetazolamide?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue those. They help with migraines and pseudotumor cerebri. Your PCP has been updated on all changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have a follow-up with my neurologist soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve scheduled you with Dr. ___ next week to review your headache management and consider other treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep monitoring your blood pressure at home, take your meds as directed, and call if the headache worsens or you have any chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our team is here for you. You’ll receive discharge instructions and prescriptions at the desk. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Headache is mild now, and I’m not feeling dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Blood pressure is 116 over 80—excellent. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad this is behind me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy, keep your follow-ups, and reach out if anything changes. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.
